title: Six Weeks in Southern Germany
paragraphs: From March to mid-April 2024, I was looked after in the neurology department of Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU) in southern Germany. I would like to look back on it, touching on my experiences in the dispatch program and my private life.

The place where I did my clerkship was Klinikum Großhadern, one of the largest hospitals in Europe, located on the outskirts of Munich. In the first half I took part in the Neurology Winter School (NWS), and in the second half I was allowed to observe a movement disorders outpatient clinic.

The Winter School schedule was ward work in the morning, a joint conference with radiology at midday, and a lecture, case discussion or lab tour in the afternoon. On the ward, I worked together with two supervising doctors, two or three medical students in their clerkship year, and an LMU student (study buddy) who also took part in the Winter School. In Germany, it seems students have hospital clerkships from the lower years of medical school. At first I felt anxious that I would fall behind the local students who were used to it, but from things I had experience in, such as physical examination and interviews of new patients, to unfamiliar procedures such as blood drawing and line placement, I got through safely with the help of my buddy, Michelle. The joint conference after lunch is a place where radiologists and neurologists gather and repeatedly discuss imaging tests. The content was all in German, so all I could do was follow the images with my eyes to see whether there were any cases from my ward. The afternoon content varied from day to day, and every day there was something new to learn, so I never got bored. When the afternoon was a lecture, professors of the specialty field gave it, and occasionally professors of related fields such as neurosurgery or emergency medicine. In most cases, after the students' self-introductions, they began with innocuous questions such as "Why did you choose this program?" and "What research field or department are you interested in?" On the other hand, answering questions asked during class such as "Isn't there a large-scale research project related to this under way in Japan?" and "Is the prevalence of this disease in Japan the same as in Europe?" was by no means easy. I regret that, since I was studying abroad, I should have prepared to discuss not only Japan and its medical care but also in comparison with other countries. There were also several Clinical Case Discussions chaired by ward doctors, and the scene in which students discussed among themselves while actually making rounds was impressive. Visits to the centres, laboratories and related facilities attached to the hospital were also attractive, and I also had the chance to go to the campus in the city centre. What remains most vividly in my memory is the one-day clerkship at a rehabilitation centre in the suburbs. Seeing unfamiliar equipment up close and actually operating it was, I think, a valuable experience that is hard to get in hospital clerkships in Japan. During the Winter School the ward was the main stage, but in the outpatient observation in the second half I was able to experience a completely different atmosphere. Although it was called observation, in fact there were several occasions on which I was allowed to perform neurological examinations under the supervision of a senior doctor, and I think it was a wonderful environment in which one could actively take part in practice if one wished. Because it was a specialised movement disorders clinic, a characteristic was that I saw several patients who, as part of research, were subjected to meticulous neurological examination, questionnaires running to many pages, and a large number of tests such as lumbar puncture and MRI. Also, the senior doctors sometimes told me about ongoing clinical trials, and I realised that it is a leading hospital in the country and at the same time a huge research facility. We examined the patients together and each time they explained to me in English, and in the afternoon, after outpatient practice ended, the senior doctor would say to me to make the most of my remaining time in Germany, and the day would end. After most of my Winter School cohort had gone home I sometimes felt lonely, but I often met Jakob from Slovenia, who also remained at the hospital, had dinner with him, and talked for hours.

Sightseeing and entertainment are the real pleasure of studying abroad, and since I spent most of the weekdays at the hospital, a break was naturally necessary. Fortunately, my private life was fulfilling too. For the participants of the NWS and the Oncology Winter School (OWS), held in parallel with the NWS, weekend trips within southern Germany had been planned in advance, and I was able to deepen friendships with students I had little contact with in the hospital. Besides that, most of the time I spent together with them, eating out after the hospital and going around bars. What left an impression among them was the beer festival (Starkbierfest) to which I was invited on the weekend of the third week. It is a festival to enjoy beer whose origin is that it was drunk in place of meals during the fasting period in March, and it was a little different from the Oktoberfest, which is well known in Japan. Of course, I could not fail to touch on the beauty of Munich. Even just strolling from the central station toward the city centre, you can catch a glimpse of its rich culture and history. Among them, Marienplatz, the most important landmark in Munich, is spectacular. The central square, where the town hall (Rathaus) stands majestically, is also a subway interchange station and the lively centre of the local economy. Around the bustling market there are lined cafes, restaurants, pubs and numerous specialty shops. On days when I wanted to relax there were plenty of other options, such as tours of the museums scattered around the city, visiting the churches around the town hall, and walking in the vast English Garden, so I was never bored.

We exchange students who took part in the Winter School were lent rooms in a dormitory in the Olympic Village. The (huge) student residential area where the dormitory is located has the necessary things, a supermarket, restaurants and bakeries, the Olympic Park, a coin laundry and a subway station (Olympiazentrum), and it was very comfortable. In particular, access to the city centre was smooth and it was convenient for commuting. The dormitory room could be used only during the Winter School, and we were asked to move out at the end of March. Fortunately, with the help of Aurelia, an LMU student friend with whom I had been in contact beforehand, I was able to rent the room of her friend Pia and spend the rest of the period.

In this dispatched clerkship, which I took on after finishing most of my clinical clerkships in Japan, I was able to test the knowledge I had acquired so far. There were scenes where I did not do well, but I think I was able to take part proactively without slacking. Thinking back now, the surrounding environment may also have contributed to my being able to take part with concentration. That is because nearly all the doctors were enthusiastic about education, and every student I met was curious and fond of discussion. Being asked about cultural differences, medical or non-medical, was very stimulating, and my heart leapt every time it developed into a complex and abstract topic. Thanks to an environment with many friendly people I was able to make friends with local students and exchange students, and there are students with whom I am still in contact. There are almost no negative descriptions so far, and some of you may be puzzled. In fact, from the outside too, I apparently spent peaceful days throughout. But although I have overseas experience, it is not that there was no trouble at all this time (although almost only language-related). Inside the hospital I could communicate in English with doctors and medical students, but outside the hospital it was not so easy. The bakery I stopped at every morning had no English menu, and each time I googled what looked delicious and ate it. Sometimes I guessed signs written in German at random, and at other times I relied on pattern recognition and made the choice I thought appropriate, and as my stay went on I increasingly acted haphazardly. Wherever you go, you should study at least the basics of the local language.

Without the many wonderful encounters up to today, I could not have gained such a valuable experience. I would like to express my gratitude to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office and MISU who gave me the opportunity for a dispatched study abroad, the doctors of the Department of Neurology at LMU, beginning with Professor Dimitriadis, the students who took part in the Winter School and the LMU students who looked after me, and my family who gave me advice.
